title: KV shelf retention curves and fragmentation mitigation
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description:
Problem statement: As continuous batching increases request concurrency, the KV cache exhibits pathological fragmentation on long-running GPU workers. Small-lived keys and churn from batched requests create many tiny free regions that reduce usable KV capacity and increase eviction frequency, hurting P99 latency and token throughput.

Proposal summary: Introduce a "KV shelf" allocation strategy that groups KV entries by expected lifetime and write-rate into retention "shelves" (short, medium, long). Each shelf uses a tailored allocation quantum and reclamation policy: short shelf uses compact slot pools with time-decay tombstones and fast in-place overwrite; medium shelf uses slab-like fixed buckets with opportunistic coalescing; long shelf uses larger contiguous segments with occasional background compaction. Combine this with a retention curve heuristic (probabilistic TTL + recency-weighting) and a lightweight fragmentation budget that triggers gentle background compaction when fragmentation crosses thresholds.

How it interacts with continuous batching and GPU memory: - Batching amplifies hot-key write amplification; assigning high-write-rate keys to the short shelf reduces churn impact on larger shelves. - Quantized allocation quanta per shelf reduce internal fragmentation vs one-size allocation. - Background compaction is scheduled respecting GPU occupancy and batching windows (compact during low-throughput windows or between micro-batches).

Design details: - Shelf classifier: runtime predictor using sliding-window stats (write-rate, last-access delta, token-length) to score keys into shelves. Lightweight: maintained in per-worker circular buffers to avoid global locks. - Allocation: short shelf uses fixed-length micro-slots (e.g., 256B/512B), medium uses medium-sized bins (2KB/8KB), long shelf allocates contiguous segments in page-aligned chunks tuned to model KV size distribution. - Reclamation: short shelf favors overwrite and quick tombstone expiry; medium shelf uses localized coalescing during low-traffic epochs; long shelf supports epochal compaction with pointer indirection for live keys to avoid large pause. - Fragmentation budget: worker-level metric computed as (free_frag_bytes / total_kv_bytes) with hysteresis windows to avoid thrashing. When budget exceeded, schedule a compaction job targeting the shelf with highest reclaimable bytes. - Telemetry hooks: expose shelf-level occupancy, per-key shelf-move frequency, compaction time, and effect on P50/P95/P99 latencies.

Trade-offs and risks: - Complexity: additional classifier and shelf bookkeeping increases CPU usage and code surface area. Mitigation: start with a single-worker prototype and microbench before cluster rollout. - Edge cases: keys migrating shelves can create short-lived double-hold of memory; mitigate via move-on-read with bounded parallelism. - Compaction cost: expensive if scheduled poorly; mitigate via fragmentation budget & GPU occupancy awareness.

Experiment plan: 1) Microbench harness (local): simulate mixed workload (50% short-lived chat KV, 30% medium, 20% long warm prefixes) and measure usable KV bytes, eviction rate, and per-token latency under continuous batching. 2) Canary rollout on staging pool with 10% traffic controlled by routing policy. 3) Monitor telemetry dashboard (kv-shelf-experiment) and rollback if P99 token latency or throughput degrades beyond 5%.

Deliverables: - RFC doc (Confluence) describing algorithm and API flags. - Microbench harness and results. - Implementation PR for runtime worker with feature-flag and opt-in config. - Console telemetry dashboard and alerts. - Runbook for tuning shelf sizes and compaction thresholds.
